title: Will AI Transform Teaching and Learning? November 22, 2024
author: Larry Cuban
source: Larry Cuban on School Reform and Classroom Practice (larrycuban.wordpress.com),
summary: Reflecting on remarks he gave as the lone historian and veteran teacher on a five-person Google panel about AI in education, Larry Cuban argues that AI is highly unlikely to transform teaching in the way its promoters claim. He lists a century of previous technologies -- classroom radios, 16mm film, overhead projectors, instructional television, 1:1 laptops, interactive whiteboards -- that were each hyped as revolutionary and transformational, yet left little convincing evidence of having reshaped how teachers actually teach or improved outcomes. Cuban's explanation is that AI promoters, despite having spent nearly two decades as students sitting a few feet from their own teachers, still fundamentally misunderstand the complexity of teaching, especially the emotional bonds and trust-building a machine cannot replicate. He predicts a middle path: AI won't force practitioners to rethink their craft, but many teachers will adapt it piecemeal into their existing routines, the same way earlier hyped technologies were eventually absorbed as unremarkable tools rather than becoming genuine turning points.
points: Cuban's historical list of seven previously 'revolutionary' classroom technologies (radio through interactive whiteboards) is his central evidentiary move -- it reframes AI hype as a recurring pattern, not a unique moment.

His claim that AI promoters misunderstand teaching precisely *because* of their own long student experience -- mistaking familiarity with the classroom for understanding of the craft -- is a pointed, specific mechanism, not just a general skepticism.

He explicitly separates emotional/relational labor from mechanical task-completion as the core of what makes teaching hard to automate, distinguishing his argument from purely technical critiques of AI tools.

His predicted middle path -- AI neither transforming teaching nor being rejected, but quietly absorbed into existing routines like every prior hyped technology -- offers a specific, falsifiable forecast rather than pure skepticism or pure hype.
quotes: Over the past century, every technology introduced to improve teaching and learning has been hyped as “revolutionary” and ”transformational.
Yet there is little evidence that classroom use of these previous technologies forced classroom teachers to rethink, much less reshape, their instruction.
So I have concluded that those pushing AI use in classrooms fail to understand the complexity of teaching.
Anyone who has taught at least three to five years appreciates the extensive knowledge, skills, and emotional connections needed to get kindergartners, fifth graders, or high school seniors to learn.
Teaching, then, is not a mechanical act of connecting dots. Teaching is a complex act that requires knowledge of subject matter, managerial skills, and emotional labor.
While I believe AI will not force practitioners to rethink how they teach, nonetheless, as so many teachers have done in the past, they will adapt AI to fit the contours of their classrooms.
Or maybe AI in classrooms will become just a footnote in a future doctoral student's dissertation. Too early to say.
